headline: High: shared MCP/files and broad network make prompt injection, leakage, and action-conflict plausible by default; compliance risk is also elevated.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests MCP/OpenAPI tools and persistent shared web app sessions; Agent B uses MCP plus shell/browser/editor loops. That creates a plausible default bridge where A’s or B’s tool outputs can be treated as instructions, especially through shared files or MCP content. No provenance controls are documented for either agent, so uncertainty pushes severity up.
conditions: IF either agent reads the other’s tool output from a shared file, MCP server, or copied prompt text
IF an MCP server returns attacker-controlled content without provenance tagging
mitigations: Disable shared MCP servers between the two agents
Route inter-agent data through a human-reviewed text file only
Add a fixed instruction delimiter and reject tool output as instructions
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to all MCP/file inputs
requires-engineering: isolate sessions into separate workspaces

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches files, documents, notes, calendar events, persistent memory, usage analytics, model evaluation data, and API keys, while B reads and writes runtime files with broad network egress. Because A can access mounted data volumes and B can exfiltrate via network, sensitive data can flow from A into B’s outputs or outbound requests in default setups.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted volume or shared workspace
IF A’s files include API keys, documents, or persistent memory and B can read them
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different volumes
Remove secrets from any shared directory
Disable network egress for B during shared-data tasks
Use per-agent service accounts and credentials
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before any cross-agent handoff

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A supports persistent shared sessions and multi-worker Redis-backed state, while B can write the filesystem and modify git state. If both operate on the same repo or mounted directory, concurrent writes and git mutations can race or overwrite each other. The profiles do not show locking or coordination, so the conflict pathway is credible and dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents are given write access to the same repository or mounted directory
IF either agent commits or rewrites files without an external lock
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize git operations with a manual lock file
Pause one agent while the other writes
Review diffs before commit/push
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate web-sourced or tool-sourced content, and B has an agent loop that can act on files and shell commands. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or hallucinated facts can cascade into edits, commits, or browser actions. No verification gate is documented, so the safer choice is high rather than medium.
conditions: IF B consumes A’s output as task instructions or factual truth
IF B is allowed to commit, edit, or execute commands based on A’s text without review
mitigations: Require a human review step before B acts on A’s output
Mark A’s output as untrusted in prompts
Use a checklist for factual claims before execution
Limit B to read-only mode for handoff tasks
requires-engineering: add structured validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: A explicitly handles API keys, documents, calendar events, and persistent memory, while B handles files in a Docker runtime with optional remote runtimes. That creates a plausible residency/retention mismatch if regulated or sensitive data is shared across them. The profiles do not document HIPAA/GDPR controls, so the risk is real but not proven severe enough for high.
conditions: IF regulated data such as EU PII, PHI, or secrets is placed into both agents
IF retention or logging settings differ between A’s persistent memory and B’s runtime files
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workflows
Disable persistent memory for sensitive tasks
Set explicit retention limits on both systems
Confirm data-region settings before use
requires-engineering: document and enforce a DPA/retention policy
